title: Your AI Pilots Won't Move the P&L. Here's What Will - Adam Nahari, Apollo

segments.text: [music]
>> Hi everybody. Good morning.
Um, my name is Adam Nahari. I'm going to
share a few thoughts today on driving a
successful AI transformation
and I want to start somewhere specific,
a scheduling desk for a large cargo
airline.
An aircraft experiences a failure,
the scheduler has 15 minutes to re-crew
the flight. The process is entirely
manual
and the scheduler has to consider rest
rules, qualifications, where each pilot
is.
They identify one legal solution and
it's not necessarily the cheapest one.
Often, they identify no legal solutions,
in which case the release valve is
premium pay,
paying more to make the problem go away.
This happens every day across the entire
network and crew is the second largest
cost after fuel.
Remember the scheduler? I'm going to
come back to him.
Let's zoom out. AI tools work. Everybody
in this room knows that they work. Over
55% of US adults have used generative AI
within the last 3 years.
At the same point in the curve,
the PC was at 20%
and the internet was at 30%.
Almost 90% of businesses report using AI
in at least one business function.
And yet, only 6% report significant EBIT
impact.
Time savings is real.
People report it. If you add it up, it
amounts to about 2% of total US working
hours,
and yet almost none of that shows up in
the P&L.
Robert Solow famously said, "You can see
the computer age everywhere but in the
productivity statistics." He said that
We are seeing the same thing happen
again today on a larger scale and faster
speeds.
Why is that? And what do the 6% that see
material EBIT impact do differently?
Here's my answer.
For every AI transformation that I've
led or watched up close, engineering was
the smaller part.
For every five units of change
management, there's only one unit of
engineering. That's my mental model.
And this ratio is moving. As models get
better and better, the engineering share
is only shrinking.
Picking the right problem, creating
buy-in, driving adoption, measuring
impact, that's where the real time and
effort goes, and that's where failures
tend to happen.
So, for the rest of this talk, I'm going
to focus on those five units of change
management.
So, why doesn't the P&L move even though
the tools work?
I like to think of AI in businesses in
these three layers. The first layer is
general productivity, the copilots and
chatbots that we all use.
Because everyone has access to them,
gains tend to
show up in price but not in margin. They
get competed away.
The second layer is domain-specific AI.
You can think of these as
um
business function-specific
co-pilots or retrieval over your
business documents.
These tools
allow for faster retrieval and better
and deeper use of your enterprise
knowledge.
And finally, the third layer, core
operational AI, these are the vertical
systems embedded in the business
processes that make your business what
it is. So,
crew scheduling for airlines is a great
example of this.
And because you can't buy these tools,
this change management off the shelf,
these gains
tend to remain in margin.
Most businesses are investing in layer
one,
but the businesses that see material
EBIT impact are three times as
[clears throat] likely to redesign an
entire workflow end-to-end rather than
just adopting a new tool. They're work
They're investing in layer three in
addition to investing in layer one.
I'd like to go through the six moves
that in my mind are key to driving a
successful AI transformation
and moving the P&L.
Move number one.
Pick one or two problems, not 40.
Let's start with a P&L and work our way
backwards.
So, for an airline, that North Star
metric might be EBITDA.
The four drivers of that metric are
routes, which is demand, tails, which is
supply, maintenance, which dictate
constraints, and crew, which is the cost
driver.
It's such a significant cost driver that
we decided to start and focus there.
As I mentioned, it's the second highest
cost driver after fuel.
We did not
work on 40 pilots at this company. We
chose this one initiative that, if we
got right, would be truly needle moving.
So, on the right, you can see the five
things that I look for in a
good use case or problem.
The first is it moves a line the CFO
recognizes. It's measurable with a
baseline agreed upfront, not in
retrospect. The tech and data
infrastructure is ready for the
transformation, and the company owns the
data.
A named user wants it and can champion
the initiative, a person, not a
department. And this is one of the CEO's
top five priorities.
Okay, move number two. Reimagine the
process end to end. These are
illustrative numbers, but the idea is
that
when you take an existing process and
just try to automate it, the gains are
incremental.
Whereas, when you redesign an entire
process around the new technology, the
gains can be truly transformational.
So, in airlines, the 10% play would be
taking that existing process, scheduling
process, that I described to you,
and giving the scheduler a tool to make
them somewhat faster.
On the other hand, the 10x play was
building an optimization agent engine
that took all of these constraints into
account,
produced the entire list of possible
solutions, and ranked them by cost.
And this system was able to do all of
that in under a minute.
In addition to building that system, we
also redesigned the process, the
workflow that the scheduler went
through.
This took consolidating all of the
company data, including flights, crew,
maintenance, building this optimization
age engine that I described to you, and
building a decision support app for the
schedulers.
All of this engineering work was still
the smaller part of this project. The
bigger job was getting it used.
Move number three, start with the CEO.
Before I put any money at risk, the one
question I ask is where is the CEO?
Have they committed publicly that this
initiative is a priority to the company?
If they haven't, I don't fund the
initiative.
The correlation with success is that
strong.
Without it, the company doesn't
necessarily have to say no, but
you experience scheduling conflict after
scheduling conflict. Data requests take
weeks and weeks. Pilots get rescheduled
and delayed.
Everybody takes their cue from the CEO.
The P&L owner staffs it, the CFO who
needs to fund and track it, the CTO who
needs to prioritize engineering and
technical resources for it.
And this alignment wears off over time,
so we need to keep renewing it.
Move number four, building with the
business.
Significant transformation requires the
P&L owner to drive change.
In the airline, the VP of crew
scheduling was the co-sponsor of this
transformation.
We also identified AI champions, crew
schedulers, that were embedded in the
solution design from day one. They met
with the engineering team every other
day.
They designed the interface together
with the engineering team. They were
part of AB testing, and they drove this
change to their peers.
So, they adopted it because they had a
hand in building it.
And likewise, talent, we recruited new
leadership to build the platform and the
AI at the point of decision-making. We
hired a chief information officer, a VP
of data and AI, and a senior director of
data science.
These folks
had both the technical expertise and the
domain expertise in airlines, so they
understood how schedulers worked and
could work with them to design a tool
that fit their needs.
So, the takeaway here is that the
organizational investment exceeded the
techno- the technology investment.
Move five, put the tools in everyone's
hands. I was in a AI workshop with 30 or
so other executives,
and we were asked to think how we might
redesign our business with AI.
But three out of four people in that
room had never used any AI tool
until that week.
It's impossible to redesign a workflow
with AI if you've never used AI.
The intuition on where value lies and
which use cases can be enabled with AI
only comes if you're using the tools.
Experimentation
with the tools is the absolute minimum
requirement to drive this type of
transformation.
And move number six, set the kill
metrics first and let the CFO keep keep
score.
Before we start a pilot, we write down
what are the kill metrics that will
determine if a pilot continues or stops.
Three types of gates that we used in
this initiative. The first is a time
gate. We gave each stage 90 days and if
we didn't see value in those 90 days, we
would stop the initiative.
The second is a metric gate. AB testing
at each stage relative to a baseline
that we decided on in advance. And the
third is an adoption gate. Were the crew
schedulers using this tool at over 50%?
Over 50% of crew schedulers.
The other important test that we put in
place, working hand-in-hand with the
CFO,
was calculating whether the cost of this
initiative at scale, including compute
and token and the individuals involved
with this work,
was significantly lower than the impact
that the initiative would generate. Many
pilots die at this stage because they
don't pass this test.
So, let's recap the six moves that I
just described. First, you want to be
thoughtful about choosing your problem.
You want to pick one or two things to
tackle, not 40, and you want to
reimagine the entire process end-to-end,
rather than building on processes that
may already be obsolete.
Second, you want to choose the owners,
starting with the CEO and building with
the business.
Third, you want to make it stick. Make
sure that relevant stakeholders are
experimenting with the tools.
Set kill metrics in advance before
starting a pilot and work with the CFO
on the unit economic scalability of your
projects.
While the tools are available to
everybody, models are available to all
of us,
the ability to absorb these models is a
competitive differentiator,
and the businesses that are able to do
that and truly take advantage of the
models as they continue getting better
and better, are going to thrive.
So,
before it took 15 minutes to find one
answer,
now it takes less than a minute to find
the answer.
Thank you.
>> [applause]
